flags.observation: "Nobody reads small print. That's why I put the truth there." exemplifies a recurring anecdote-plus-aphorism structure repeated across many beats.
"Your nervous system thinks that is death. It is not." states an abstract psychological claim flatly, without the concrete grounding used elsewhere.
"Last time it was me and a thermos, so this is a movement." references an unestablished prior event the standalone piece never otherwise supplies.
"A pigeon, an emu, a duck and a crow huddled over a coffee carafe" shifts into whimsical animal imagery, tonally distinct from the grounded human narrative around it.
"improvement often looks like mild disobedience to a stuck system" repeats the same anecdote-then-maxim pattern seen in multiple earlier beats, adding to a formulaic feel.
"Stay Fluffy, Folks!" closes the piece with a tag line unconnected to the protopia, slat, or armchair imagery built up earlier.

individuality.observation: The armchair conceit, "doom, one says saved", recurs and resolves in the outro, and concrete props like "the bench has a loose slat" keep the satire specific rather than generic self-help language.

outro.observation: "Who's clapping? Stop that." lands as a sharp self-aware callback, but the closing "Stay Fluffy, Folks!" reads as a stock sign-off disconnected from the protopia and slat material built up before it.

performer.observation: A dry, self-deprecating voice carries the whole piece, shown in "Yes, I made the flyer myself, and yes, it's ugly." Consistent diction and wit sustain one recognizable personality throughout.

standalone.observation: The piece defines its own central term on the spot, as in "Some people call it protopia. I call it Saturday." No outside knowledge of a deck or prior song is assumed anywhere.

storyBetweenCards.observation: A weekday-by-weekday arc runs from flyers through doors, the Saturday repair, Sunday logging, to Monday's crossing stripe, giving the cards real sequence and cause-and-effect rather than a loose list.

transferable.observation: Recurring concrete props such as "the bench has a loose slat" and "the hinge on the hall" anchor the piece to one specific street story, limiting how far it could move to another topic.

lyrics:
[Spoken Word]

Wednesday, eleven at night, one staple gun, two hundred flyers. If you walked home tonight, you've seen one. Sorry about your lamppost.

Every living room on this street has two armchairs. One says doom, one says saved. Both very comfortable. The third option has no chair. Some people call it protopia. I call it Saturday.

Yes, I made the flyer myself, and yes, it's ugly. Make the first version bad on purpose. Bad is how you know it is real.

Small print at the bottom: the future is a process of slow, incremental improvement you participate in. Nobody reads small print. That's why I put the truth there.

Time and place in pencil, because pencil means you expect to be wrong and stay anyway.

And on top, in letters you can read from a bus: The Invitation. Turn watching into showing up. Name a time, a place, a task. Saturday, nine, the bench by the bus stop. Bring gloves.

Thursday I did the doors.

First door, a prickly man. I said hi. You lower the bar to contact. Most cooperation starts embarrassingly small. He said hi back.

Second door, lights on, nothing. They might not respond. Your nervous system thinks that is death. It is not.

Third door, a wrench and a terrible hat. Authority is overrated, proximity is underrated. Ask the one who actually does the thing.

Turns out real know-how is often badly dressed and lives three doors down.

After that I knocked first everywhere. Go first. Every ally was a stranger until somebody did.

Saturday, nine. Four of them came. Last time it was me and a thermos, so this is a movement.

A pigeon, an emu, a duck and a crow huddled over a coffee carafe: the first small, clumsy gathering. Clumsy is the entry fee.

The bench has a loose slat, so that's our one broken thing close enough to touch.

Not world peace. A slat. A repair you can finish this week, not a revolution you can only announce.

Eight hands, one slat, and we split a problem the way your ancestors raised a barn.

Somebody checks the news. Phone down. Take the one breath the feed is built to deny you.

Done by ten. Nobody filmed it, because small fixes do not trend. They just hold.

Next week, the hinge on the hall. One repair a week is fifty-two a year. Nobody clapped, and the place is different.

Sunday I wrote it all down.

Write down what you actually saw, not what the headline said you would see.

Count the whole thing, including the times it worked and nobody noticed.

Monday, the crossing by the school. Three years of petitions, no stripe.

There's a little white stripe there now. No idea who. Run a tiny version. Low stakes, real feedback, no permission needed.

Strictly speaking, improvement often looks like mild disobedience to a stuck system.

Back to the armchairs.

The Comfort of Maybe: trade the warm baths of hopeless and handled for the cold shower of it depends on us.

And there is no final version. The cost is showing up again next week.

Nobody will clap. Start anyway. The clapping was never the point.

[Applause]

Who's clapping? Stop that. Forget the brochure. Ignore the loop. Pick up the pencil.

Doom gets the subscriptions. Rescue gets the tickets. A Saturday with a loose slat earns nothing, which is how you know it's yours.

Same bench, next week, nine. Bring gloves.

Stay Fluffy, Folks!

One warm female alto, talking fast and a little out of breath, then landing each line with a smile; short group answers on a few phrases. Sunny live-room mix, everything audible, nothing polished.
